name: Rivastigmine (Exelon)
summary: Cholinesterase inhibitor used for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia. Can help cognition and, for some people, reduce hallucinations, agitation, and delirium—but GI side effects and weight loss are common, especially with fast titration.
description: Rivastigmine is a brain acetylcholine booster used in Alzheimer’s dementia and Parkinson’s disease dementia. In psychiatry-world, it’s most relevant when dementia comes with hallucinations, agitation, or fluctuating confusion. The patch often causes less nausea than pills, but you still have to titrate slowly. Watch for weight loss, dizziness, fainting, and slow heart rate. Never wear more than one patch at a time—patch errors have caused overdoses.
patient_summary: Rivastigmine is used for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia and sometimes helps hallucinations, agitation, and delirium. The patch is usually easier on the stomach than capsules, but you still have to go slow. The biggest issues are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, dizziness, and fainting—especially during dose increases. Only wear ONE patch at a time and remove the old patch before putting on a new one.

primary_indications: Dementia of the Alzheimer type (mild to moderate for oral; mild to severe for transdermal)
Mild to moderate dementia associated with Parkinson disease

linked_conditions.context: Used to support cognition and daily functioning in Alzheimer’s dementia; the transdermal patch is used across mild, moderate, and severe stages.
FDA-labeled for mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease dementia; clinically relevant for hallucinations, fluctuations, and cognitive slowing.
Often used when Lewy body dementia is driving hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, or behavioral symptoms.
Sometimes used as a backup option for anticholinergic delirium when physostigmine is unavailable, typically with toxicology guidance.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to rivastigmine, other carbamate derivatives, or any component of the formulation
History of application-site reactions with rivastigmine patch

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Not a “feel it in an hour” medication; benefits are gradual and modest
efficacy_response.patient_text: Rivastigmine isn’t a fast sedative or a quick fix. When it helps, it tends to show up over weeks as steadier thinking, less confusion, and sometimes fewer hallucinations or less agitation—especially in Parkinson’s disease dementia or Lewy body dementia.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral: rapid; Transdermal: gradual steady delivery
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral: within ~1 hour; Patch: begins within 30-60 minutes but clinical effects are gradual over weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: ~1 hour; Patch: ~8-16 hours after first application
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: ~1.5 hours; Patch: ~3 hours after removal
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Central anticholinesterase activity can persist for ~10 hours after a 6 mg oral dose
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily via cholinesterase-mediated hydrolysis; CYP involvement is minimal
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food delays absorption and lowers peak levels; take oral doses with meals to improve tolerability

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Rivastigmine is a dementia medication. In psychiatry-land, it matters most when cognitive decline is tangled up with hallucinations, agitation, sleep-wake disruption, and episodes of fluctuating confusion (especially Parkinson’s disease dementia and Lewy body dementia). It’s not an anxiolytic, not an antidepressant, and not a sleep med—any calming effect is usually indirect (less confusion, fewer hallucinations), not a direct sedation effect.
items: {link:condition:alzheimer-disease:Alzheimer’s dementia}: Supports cognition and daily functioning (oral for mild to moderate; patch for mild to severe)
{link:condition:parkinson-disease-dementia:Parkinson’s disease dementia}: Supports cognition and can sometimes reduce hallucinations and fluctuations
off_label: Dementia with Lewy bodies (hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, behavioral symptoms)
Severe Alzheimer’s dementia using the oral formulation (some clinicians use; labeling differs by formulation)
Anticholinergic delirium as an alternative when physostigmine is unavailable (specialist/toxicology-guided use)
Vascular dementia when there’s suspected mixed dementia (comorbid Alzheimer’s/Parkinson’s/Lewy body features)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Rivastigmine isn’t a “kick in” medication. If it helps, it’s usually subtle and gradual. These are the patterns people describe most often:

quotes: It wasn’t night-and-day, but I had more ‘good hours’ in the day.
Less fog. I felt more present in conversations.
The confusion didn’t disappear, but it felt less chaotic.
The scary visual stuff happened less often.
Fewer ‘episodes’ where everything felt unreal or confusing.
It didn’t erase hallucinations, but it lowered the intensity.
items.note: This isn’t guaranteed, but rivastigmine is commonly chosen when dementia symptoms include hallucinations and big fluctuations.

quotes: Nausea hit hard when the dose went up.
I’d be fine for a bit, then the diarrhea showed up.
The patch was way easier than the pills for my stomach.
items.note: GI side effects are dose-related and often show up during titration.

quotes: I felt lightheaded standing up—like my body lagged behind me.
More tired than usual at first.
I had a couple near-faints and we had to slow down.
items.note: Dizziness, fainting, and slow heart rate can happen—especially in older adults or people on other heart-rate-lowering meds.

quotes: If I forget to take pills, the patch is a lifesaver.
The skin got red and itchy, so we had to rotate spots better.
The #1 rule: remove the old patch before putting on the new one.
items.note: Patch errors (wearing more than one) can cause overdose-level side effects.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Rivastigmine starts changing brain chemistry quickly, but clinical benefits (thinking, behavior, hallucinations) usually take weeks and depend on slow titration.
key_points: Oral: absorbed quickly; peak levels around ~1 hour after a dose
Patch: medication starts absorbing within 30-60 minutes, but reaches peak levels much later (often 8-16 hours after first application)
Clinical changes are gradual: expect weeks, not hours
Central anticholinesterase activity can persist for ~10 hours after a 6 mg oral dose
If you stop for more than a few days, you usually need to restart low and retitrate to avoid intense side effects

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Cognition and behavioral symptom support over time
sections.comparison: Best outcomes when titrated slowly and tolerated
sections.text: Rivastigmine can help stabilize cognition and day-to-day functioning in dementia, and it may also help neuropsychiatric symptoms that ride along with dementia—like hallucinations, agitation, and fluctuating confusion—especially in Parkinson’s disease dementia and Lewy body dementia. The tradeoff is tolerability: if the dose climbs too fast (or restarts too high after missed doses), nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and weight loss can wipe out any benefit.
sections.clinical_details: Clinically, rivastigmine is often chosen when dementia symptoms include hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations, and when antipsychotics are risky or poorly tolerated (common in Lewy body spectrum disorders). Benefit is typically assessed over weeks to months, with dose increases spaced out to protect tolerability.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Patch safety rule: wear ONE patch at a time—remove the old patch before applying the new one.
other: GI side effects are common and dose-related (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); dehydration and weight loss can follow
Bradycardia, fainting, and conduction problems can occur (especially in older adults or people with heart disease)
May worsen tremor or other extrapyramidal symptoms in Parkinson’s disease
Patch reactions can range from mild irritation to allergic dermatitis; severe skin reactions require stopping
CNS effects can include dizziness, drowsiness, and impaired alertness—use caution with driving until you know your response
MRI caution: patches may contain metal—remove the patch before MRI per product guidance
patient_counseling: If you’re using the patch: remove the old patch before putting on a new one. No doubling up—ever.
Titrate slowly. Most side effects happen when the dose increases or when restarting after a break.
Take oral doses with meals to reduce nausea.
Report fainting, slow pulse, chest symptoms, severe dizziness, or new/worsening confusion.
Track weight. If appetite drops or weight is trending down, that’s a big deal—tell your clinician.
Rotate patch sites and don’t re-use the same skin spot for about 2 weeks to reduce irritation.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, and weight loss—especially with oral dosing or fast titration. Also watch for dizziness, fainting, slow heart rate, and patch skin reactions.
plain_language_list: Agitation or restlessness can occur (especially reported with the patch in some patients)
Patch redness/itching at the application site (transdermal)

common.incidence: Oral: nausea ~23-47%; vomiting ~17-31% (rates vary by dose and titration speed)
common.patient_note: This is the #1 reason people quit or need to slow down. It often spikes right after a dose increase or a too-fast restart. Taking oral doses with meals and titrating slowly helps. The patch tends to be gentler on the stomach.
Diarrhea can lead to dehydration, weakness, and confusion—especially in older adults. If diarrhea is persistent, the plan is usually to pause, step back to a lower dose, and retitrate.

common.incidence: Weight loss ~1-7% reported; appetite decrease commonly reported
common.patient_note: Weight loss isn’t just a cosmetic side effect in dementia—it can worsen frailty, falls, and overall outcomes. Low body weight increases exposure and toxicity risk, so weight should be tracked.
Lightheadedness, near-fainting, or true fainting can happen—especially if rivastigmine slows the heart rate or lowers blood pressure responses. Falls are a major concern.

common.incidence: Agitation reported (patch range includes up to ~14%); insomnia can occur
common.patient_note: It’s a dementia med, but it can still make someone feel wired or restless. If behavior worsens after a dose increase, it may be the medication (or the dose) and needs reassessment.

common.incidence: Application-site erythema and itching are common; severe irritation is less common
common.patient_note: Mild redness is common. Allergic contact dermatitis is different: it spreads, swells, or persists, and usually means stopping the patch. Rotate sites and avoid irritated or broken skin.

serious: Bradycardia, heart block, QT prolongation, and rare torsades de pointes: fainting, palpitations, collapse—EMERGENCY symptoms require urgent evaluation.
Severe vomiting with dehydration or complications: persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, confusion, weakness—urgent care risk.
Severe skin reactions (including widespread allergic dermatitis or rare severe cutaneous reactions): stop and seek medical care.
Seizures (rare): new seizure activity requires urgent evaluation.
Overdose from patch errors (wearing multiple patches or not removing old patch): severe nausea/vomiting, sweating, slow heart rate, confusion, collapse—urgent evaluation.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Rivastigmine’s biggest interaction story is pharmacology (cholinergic vs anticholinergic) and additive heart-rate effects—not CYP metabolism.

items.with: Anticholinergic medications (diphenhydramine, benztropine, oxybutynin, some antipsychotics with strong anticholinergic effects, TCAs like amitriptyline)
items.risk: Pharmacologic tug-of-war: anticholinergics can blunt rivastigmine benefit and worsen confusion; combining can increase delirium risk and side effects.
items.action: Minimize anticholinergic burden whenever possible, especially in dementia. If anticholinergic delirium is being treated, rivastigmine may be used in select cases with specialist guidance.

items.with: Beta-blockers and other heart-rate-lowering meds (and other drugs that affect conduction)
items.risk: Additive bradycardia and syncope risk; conduction abnormalities are a known risk with cholinesterase inhibitors.
items.action: Use caution and monitor pulse, dizziness, and fainting. Consider ECG risk assessment in high-risk patients.

items.risk: Additive cholinergic side effects (GI toxicity, bradycardia) without clear added benefit.
items.action: Avoid combining cholinesterase inhibitors. If switching, follow a clinician-directed plan.

items.with: NSAIDs or history of ulcer disease
items.risk: Cholinergic activity can increase gastric acid secretion, potentially increasing bleeding/ulcer risk in susceptible patients.
items.action: Use caution, monitor for GI bleeding symptoms, and reassess if abdominal pain, black stools, or anemia symptoms appear.

items.with: Heat exposure on patch (sauna, prolonged external heat)
items.risk: Heat can increase absorption and side effects from the patch.
items.action: Avoid prolonged heat exposure over the patch area and follow patch handling guidance.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Rivastigmine does not cause benzodiazepine-style withdrawal. The main risk of stopping is symptom rebound: cognition, hallucinations, or confusion may worsen back toward baseline. If therapy is interrupted for more than a few days, you typically need to restart at a low dose and retitrate—because side effects can hit hard if you jump back to the old dose.
key_points: If stopped: dementia symptoms may gradually worsen back toward baseline (or progress due to disease course).
No classic dependence syndrome, but sudden discontinuation can still destabilize behavior in some patients.
If oral therapy is interrupted for >3 days: restart at 1.5 mg twice daily and retitrate.
If patch therapy is interrupted for >3 days: restart at 4.6 mg/24 hours and retitrate.
If stopping due to side effects: clinicians often pause for several doses, then restart at the same or lower dose with slower titration.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Rivastigmine dosing is slow on purpose. Going too fast is the fastest way to get nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and weight loss—especially in low body weight patients. Oral is typically twice daily with meals; the patch is once daily and often better tolerated.

adult.alzheimer_oral_initial: 1.5 mg PO twice daily with meals
adult.alzheimer_oral_titration: Increase every 2 to 4 weeks by 1.5 mg per dose (total +3 mg/day) as tolerated
adult.alzheimer_oral_target: 3 to 6 mg PO twice daily (6 to 12 mg/day total) based on tolerability and benefit
adult.alzheimer_oral_max: 6 mg PO twice daily (12 mg/day total)
adult.alzheimer_patch_initial: Apply 4.6 mg/24 hours patch once daily; remove old patch and replace every 24 hours
adult.alzheimer_patch_titration: After at least 4 weeks, increase to 9.5 mg/24 hours if tolerated; after an additional at least 4 weeks, may increase further
adult.parkinsons_dementia_oral_initial: 1.5 mg PO twice daily with meals
adult.parkinsons_dementia_oral_titration: Increase at intervals of at least 4 weeks by 1.5 mg per dose (total +3 mg/day) as tolerated
adult.parkinsons_dementia_oral_max: 6 mg PO twice daily (12 mg/day total)
adult.parkinsons_dementia_patch_initial: Apply 4.6 mg/24 hours patch once daily; replace every 24 hours
adult.parkinsons_dementia_patch_titration: After at least 4 weeks, increase to 9.5 mg/24 hours if tolerated; after at least 4 additional weeks, may increase further if beneficial and tolerated
adult.parkinsons_dementia_patch_effective_rang: 9.5 mg/24 hours or 13.3 mg/24 hours patch once daily (doses above 13.3 mg/24 hours increase adverse effects without clear added benefit)
adult.lewy_body_dementia_oral_initial: 1.5 mg PO twice daily with meals
adult.lewy_body_dementia_oral_titration: Increase every 2 weeks by 1.5 mg per dose (total +3 mg/day) as tolerated
adult.lewy_body_dementia_oral_max: 6 mg PO twice daily (12 mg/day total)
adult.anticholinergic_delirium_oral_initial: 3 to 6 mg PO once; may repeat every 1 to 2 hours until delirium improves
adult.anticholinergic_delirium_patch: Apply 9.5 mg/24 hours or 13.3 mg/24 hours patch once daily until delirium improves (toxicology-guided; ensure each patch is removed after 24 hours)
adult.conversion_oral_to_patch: If total oral daily dose is <6 mg/day, switch to 4.6 mg/24 hours patch; if total oral daily dose is 6 to 12 mg/day, switch to 9.5 mg/24 hours patch. Apply patch the day after the last oral dose.
adult.missed_doses_oral: If interrupted for ≤3 days, restart at same or lower dose and continue titration as appropriate. If interrupted for >3 days, restart at 1.5 mg PO twice daily and retitrate.
adult.missed_doses_patch: If interrupted for ≤3 days, restart at same or lower patch strength and retitrate as appropriate. If interrupted for >3 days, restart at 4.6 mg/24 hours patch and retitrate. Do not apply two patches to make up for missed doses.

sections.simple_explanation: Oral rivastigmine is taken twice daily with meals and titrated slowly to reduce nausea. The patch is once daily and often causes fewer GI side effects, but you still have to increase gradually. If you stop for more than a few days, restarting at the prior dose can trigger intense side effects—so you usually restart low and work back up.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Rivastigmine is primarily used in older adults, but special population considerations matter because side effects like dehydration, weight loss, fainting, and skin reactions can be high-stakes in frail patients.
sections.pregnancy: Human pregnancy data are limited. Animal studies have not shown clear adverse reproductive outcomes, but dementia treatment during pregnancy is uncommon. Use only if clearly needed and guided by specialist risk-benefit discussion.
sections.lactation: It is not known whether rivastigmine is present in breast milk. The decision to breastfeed during therapy should weigh potential infant exposure, benefits of breastfeeding, and benefits of treatment to the mother.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing, but monitor closely. Older adults can be more vulnerable to bradycardia, syncope, falls, dehydration, and weight loss. Oral clearance may be reduced in older adults; titrate slowly and reassess function, weight, and vital signs regularly.
sections.hepatic: Oral: clearance can be reduced in hepatic impairment; a conservative approach is slower titration and potentially lower starting frequency (for example, 1.5 mg once daily with cautious titration). Patch: in mild to moderate hepatic impairment, an initial and maximum dose of 4.6 mg/24 hours is recommended in some guidance; severe hepatic impairment has not been well studied.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally required for any degree of kidney impairment for oral or transdermal therapy, but exposure can be higher in some patients; monitor tolerability.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Cognitive function and day-to-day functioning at periodic intervals (is there meaningful benefit?)
Neuropsychiatric symptoms relevant to psychiatry care: hallucinations, agitation, sleep-wake disruption, fluctuating confusion, and distress (track baseline and changes after titration)
GI intolerance: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain—especially during titration or after restarts
Weight and appetite: baseline weight and ongoing monitoring; intervene early if weight is trending down
Hydration status: watch for dehydration (weakness, confusion, low intake, orthostasis), especially if GI side effects occur
Cardiac effects: pulse, dizziness, syncope; consider ECG risk evaluation in high-risk patients (conduction disease, beta-blocker use, arrhythmia history)
Falls and balance: increased risk if dizziness, bradycardia, or orthostasis occurs
Parkinsonism/extrapyramidal symptoms: tremor or rigidity can worsen in Parkinson’s disease
Skin reactions with patch: irritation vs allergic dermatitis; ensure rotation of sites and proper application technique
Medication administration safety: confirm only one patch is used at a time and old patch is removed before applying a new one

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Formulation choice is often about tolerability and adherence: oral can work well but causes more GI side effects for many people; the patch is once daily and often easier on the stomach.
items: Oral capsules: 1.5 mg, 3 mg, 4.5 mg, 6 mg
Transdermal patch (24 hour): 4.6 mg/24 hours, 9.5 mg/24 hours, 13.3 mg/24 hours

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Rivastigmine works by blocking the enzymes that break down acetylcholine in the brain. Acetylcholine is a key “signal” chemical for attention, learning, and memory. In Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia, acetylcholine signaling is often low. By slowing acetylcholine breakdown, rivastigmine boosts cholinergic activity—and that can translate into steadier thinking and sometimes fewer hallucinations or less fluctuating confusion in certain dementia syndromes.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Rivastigmine is not a primary psychiatry medication, but it shows up constantly in real-world psychiatric care because dementia symptoms are often behavioral. In Lewy body spectrum disorders (Parkinson’s disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies), rivastigmine is frequently favored when hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations drive distress—and when antipsychotics are risky or poorly tolerated. The patch is often the practical choice in patients who forget pills or can’t tolerate oral GI effects. The big clinical skill is pacing: slow titration, careful restarts after missed doses, and relentless monitoring of weight, hydration, falls, and heart-rate-related symptoms.

seo.title: Rivastigmine (Exelon): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Patch Safety & Delirium
seo.description: Rivastigmine (Exelon) for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease dementia: dosing for capsules and patch, side effects (nausea, weight loss, dizziness), heart-rate risks, patch safety rules, and psychiatry-relevant uses like hallucinations and delirium.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Rivastigmine is used for dementia of the Alzheimer type and for mild to moderate dementia associated with Parkinson’s disease. In real-world psych care, it’s especially relevant when dementia comes with hallucinations, agitation, or fluctuating confusion—common in Parkinson’s disease dementia and Lewy body dementia.

faqs.q: Is rivastigmine an anxiety medication or a sleep medication?
faqs.a: No. Rivastigmine is a dementia medication. If someone seems calmer on it, that’s usually because they’re less confused or having fewer hallucinations—not because it’s a sedative or a direct anti-anxiety drug.

faqs.q: How long does rivastigmine take to work?
faqs.a: The medicine starts absorbing quickly (especially oral), but meaningful changes—like steadier attention, less confusion, or fewer hallucinations—usually take weeks. It’s a slow-build medication, and the dose is increased slowly for tolerability.

faqs.q: Capsules vs patch: which is better?
faqs.a: It depends on tolerability and adherence. Capsules are taken twice daily with meals and can cause more nausea and vomiting. The patch is once daily and is often easier on the stomach, and it’s helpful when someone forgets pills. Either way, slow titration is the key.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, and weight loss—especially during dose increases. Dizziness and fainting can happen too, which matters a lot because of fall risk in older adults.

Yes. Appetite suppression and weight loss can happen, and this is a serious monitoring point in dementia care. If weight is dropping, the plan is usually to slow titration, reduce dose, switch formulations (often to the patch), or stop if the risk outweighs the benefit.

faqs.q: Can rivastigmine cause fainting or slow heart rate?
faqs.a: Yes. Cholinesterase inhibitors can increase vagal tone and slow the heart rate. Some people get dizziness, near-fainting, or syncope—especially if they already have heart conduction issues or take other medications that slow heart rate (like beta-blockers).

Only wear ONE patch at a time. Remove the old patch before applying the new one. Patch errors (like doubling up) can cause overdose-level side effects—severe vomiting, sweating, slow heart rate, confusion, and collapse.

faqs.q: What happens if we miss doses for a few days?
faqs.a: If therapy is interrupted for more than 3 days, you usually have to restart at the lowest dose and retitrate. Restarting at the previous dose after a break is a common way people get slammed with nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and dehydration.

faqs.q: Does rivastigmine help hallucinations in Lewy body dementia or Parkinson’s disease dementia?
faqs.a: It can. It’s commonly used in Lewy body spectrum disorders where hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations are part of the picture. It doesn’t work for everyone, and it’s not a replacement for a full treatment plan, but it’s often a first medication clinicians try before escalating to higher-risk options.

Sometimes, but this is a niche situation. Rivastigmine has been used as an alternative for anticholinergic delirium when physostigmine isn’t available, typically with poison center or clinical toxicology guidance. The ideal dosing strategy isn’t firmly established, so this isn’t a DIY scenario.
